profiles.meeting_scenario: A corresponding author and a practice-based coauthor meet to troubleshoot why a draft law paper on dispute resolution mechanisms for construction contract disputes received internal review comments saying the comparative-analysis chapter is inconsistent, the case section feels mismatched to the doctrinal section, and the proposed 'document mediation-arbitration-litigation' mechanism is not clearly framed. The meeting takes place at a university-affiliated construction law research center three weeks before journal resubmission. Their agenda is to diagnose why the draft currently reads as if it is describing different systems at once, identify the root cause of the mismatch between legal analysis and case evidence, and agree on a revision approach for the mechanism chapter and case-selection method. The expected outcome is a shared revision plan covering which authorities count as the current legal framework, what materials count as practical cases, how to position document mediation, and what standard will be used to decide that the chapter is 'fixed.'

members.name: Prof. Li Wen
members.role: Corresponding author and professor of civil and commercial law
members.expertise: Contract doctrine, judicial interpretation, comparative private law methodology
members.background: Li teaches construction contract law at a major law school, has published extensively on Civil Code application, and usually writes articles that rely on published judgments and formal legal sources.
members.private_state: Li wants the paper to survive strict doctrinal peer review and be publishable in a leading legal journal; he is concerned that the draft currently looks methodologically loose and that practice-heavy material could make the argument seem insufficiently grounded in formal law.
hidden_assumptions: When a legal paper says 'practical cases,' it should mainly rely on published judgments or officially disclosed decisions that can be cited and generalized from.

The 'current legal provisions' for a doctrinal paper primarily means nationally binding sources in force now, such as the Civil Code, Arbitration Law, Civil Procedure Law, and current SPC judicial interpretations.
If 'document mediation' appears in the mechanism, it should be framed as a distinct pre-adjudicative dispute-resolution step rather than an internal case-management technique.

A dispute-resolution mechanism is adequately shown to 'work' if the paper presents a doctrinally coherent sequence with lawful entry points and legally defensible transitions between mediation, arbitration, and litigation.

members.name: Chen Yu
members.role: Construction disputes senior associate and external research collaborator
members.expertise: Construction arbitration, claims management, adjudication strategy, enforcement risk
members.background: Chen practices at a commercial law firm, regularly handles contractor payment, variation, and delay disputes, and contributes empirical examples and procedural insights from arbitration commissions and court-connected practice.
members.private_state: Chen wants the paper to reflect how construction disputes are actually handled and to avoid a mechanism that looks elegant on paper but is unusable in live matters; he is concerned that the current draft underuses operational rules and real case patterns.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper refers to 'practical cases,' it naturally includes arbitral case summaries, mediation outcomes, and anonymized firm files if they reveal stable dispute-resolution patterns.

The 'current legal framework' in construction disputes includes not only national statutes but also local high court guidance, arbitration commission rules, and widely followed operational practices because these materially shape outcomes.
In construction practice, 'document mediation' usually means structured documentary exchange and issue narrowing inside an existing arbitration or court track, not a stand-alone legal stage.
A dispute-resolution mechanism counts as 'workable' if it reduces delay, narrows valuation fights, and improves the chance of a collectible, enforceable result for the parties.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss adding or reorganizing the paper's 'practical cases' section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of published court judgments and officially disclosed decisions that can be formally cited in a doctrinal article.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a broader pool including arbitral summaries, mediation outcomes, and anonymized matter files from practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal research meetings, 'practical cases' is a familiar umbrella phrase and both categories feel plausibly case-based; because both are trying to strengthen empirical support, the surface agreement sounds complete even though they are silently pointing to different evidentiary pools.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the 'current legal provisions' section
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the chapter should be aligned with the 'current legal provisions' or 'current rules.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this section should be limited to nationally binding law currently in force, with local guidance mentioned only marginally if at all.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the section should also include local high court guidance, arbitration commission procedural rules, and other operational norms that decision-makers actually use in construction disputes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Lawyers often use 'current rules' as shorthand without restating the hierarchy of sources, and both members are accustomed to their own professional defaults; because neither is rejecting the importance of law, the boundary issue stays invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the mechanism to 'work'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the revised dispute-resolution mechanism must be 'workable' or must 'work.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the mechanism is successful if the article shows a normatively coherent legal pathway among document mediation, arbitration, and litigation that can withstand doctrinal critique.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the mechanism is successful if it shortens the dispute cycle, narrows technical valuation issues, and leads to enforceable payment outcomes in real projects.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'workable mechanism' is positively valenced and broad enough to cover both doctrinal coherence and practical efficiency; because the two standards are complementary rather than openly conflicting, neither participant senses a need to specify the benchmark.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'document mediation' is in the proposed model
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to retain 'document mediation' in the proposed resolution mechanism.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes document mediation is a separate, front-end resolution channel based on documentary review before parties proceed to arbitration or litigation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes document mediation is a documentary issue-narrowing process embedded within arbitration or litigation case management rather than a separate procedural stage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase already sounds technical and specific, so each assumes the other is using the standard professional meaning; since both support keeping it in the paper, the conversation produces false consensus instead of clarification.

turns.inner_thought: The reviewers are right that the chapter reads as if it stitched together different research logics. The doctrinal analysis is built on formal sources and published judgments, but the examples section drifts into practice description in a way that will look soft to a top legal journal. If we do not tighten the evidentiary base and define a legally coherent pathway, the piece will fail peer review. By practical cases, I mean citable judgments or officially disclosed decisions. And when I say the mechanism must work, I mean the article must show a lawful sequence with defensible transitions.
turns.utterance: I think the internal review comments are essentially pointing to one problem: the chapter does not yet read as one integrated system. The practical cases, the legal analysis, and the proposed mechanism seem to be speaking in slightly different voices. If we want this version to stand, we need the whole chapter to point in one direction and show that the mechanism really works.

turns.inner_thought: That is exactly the issue from the practice side too. The patterns are there, especially in payment and variation disputes, but the draft doesn't let the reader see how disputes actually move. By practical cases, I include arbitral summaries, mediation outcomes, and anonymized firm matters, because those are often more representative than published court decisions alone. And document mediation, as I understand it, is the documentary issue-narrowing process inside a live track, which is often what keeps these disputes from ballooning before the hearing.
turns.utterance: Yes, I had the same reaction. The practical cases do show a fairly stable pattern, especially in payment and variation disputes, and document mediation is part of that pattern because it helps narrow the issues before the matter fully escalates. Right now, though, that logic is not coming through consistently on the page.

turns.inner_thought: The cleanest repair is to rebuild the chapter from the nationally binding framework outward: Civil Code, Arbitration Law, Civil Procedure Law, and current SPC interpretations. That will re-anchor the comparative discussion. If we start bringing too many practice materials or local texts into the main structure, the doctrinal line will blur again.
turns.utterance: Then perhaps the first fix is structural. We should reorganize the chapter strictly around the current legal provisions first, and let the rest of the discussion follow that order. If the framework is set by the current legal provisions, the comparative chapter should stop drifting.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that, so long as 'current rules' is understood realistically. In construction disputes, parties do not move only by statute. Local high court guidance, arbitration commission rules, and procedural habits shape what actually happens and what outcomes are reachable. If those are omitted, the chapter will look clean but detached from real dispute handling.
turns.utterance: I agree with that in principle. I would just suggest that the current rules section should reflect the full set of current rules the parties actually face in construction disputes, so that the framework does not become too abstract. If we align the chapter that way, the later sections should connect much better.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he agrees on using the formal framework. Next, the cases should be recoded by stages: mediation, arbitration, litigation. That will let me show a neat doctrinal comparison across each path. Document mediation should appear as its own front-end channel, then movement to arbitration or litigation. If the cases are grouped that way, the mechanism chapter will finally look orderly.
turns.utterance: On the evidence side, I think we should recode the practical cases by mediation, arbitration, and litigation. Once they are sorted in that way, the mechanism section should become much cleaner and also easier to compare on a doctrinal level.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me as a chapter organization, but some of the strongest practical cases are not published court judgments. They are arbitration matters and anonymized project files, and in many of them document mediation happened through rounds of document exchange and issue-list narrowing before the hearing. Those examples are exactly what will make the model usable for practitioners.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Several of the strongest practical cases we have are in arbitration matters and project files, and in those materials document mediation appears very clearly before the hearing in a way that helps narrow the dispute. If we reorganize them carefully, that pattern should become much more visible.

turns.inner_thought: For the journal, we do not need to prove practical efficiency in every dimension. We need to show legal coherence: who can enter document mediation, on what basis, and how the transition to arbitration or litigation occurs without doctrinal rupture. If that chain is clear, the mechanism counts as workable.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And to my mind, the paper only needs to demonstrate that the mechanism works by showing the lawful entry conditions and a coherent handoff between document mediation, arbitration, and litigation. If those links are clear, the chapter will feel much more settled.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that is the right direction, but readers from the disputes field will still expect the mechanism to show operational value. For me, workable means cutting a valuation round, reducing delay, and improving the odds of a collectible payment outcome. If the final chapter conveys that, people will believe it is not just elegant drafting.
turns.utterance: Exactly, and readers will also find the mechanism workable if they can see that it reduces delay, cuts down one round of valuation fighting, and moves the parties faster toward an enforceable payment result. If we can make that practical effect visible, the mechanism will land much better.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we are aligned. I will redraw the mechanism chart with document mediation as the opening module, followed by arbitration and then litigation where necessary. Chen can provide more practical cases, ideally ones that can be fitted under the current legal provisions table without upsetting the doctrinal hierarchy. If we execute that, the chapter should survive review.
turns.utterance: Then let us do this concretely. I will revise the chart so that document mediation appears as the opening module, and you can send me additional practical cases that fit the current rules table. Once those two pieces are aligned, I think the chapter will read far more coherently.

turns.inner_thought: That division of labor is fine. I will send arbitration commission materials, local guidance, and case summaries from practice, because those are the materials that show how the process really runs and why the mechanism is workable. Once those are folded in, the paper should finally reflect the live dispute environment rather than just the black-letter structure.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I will send over materials on the current rules along with practical cases and case summaries that should make the mechanism more workable in the final draft. Once you have those, we should be able to tighten the whole section fairly quickly.
